title: Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility
pass_4_primary_concern: The notice does not fully connect its selected RFE and site-visit evidence to a universal no-deference rule or explain safeguards and monitoring for the resulting burden.
pass_5_high_stakes_domain_reason: The rule affects immigration-benefit adjudications, employment authorization continuity, and the authorized stay of nonimmigrant workers.
pass_5_concise_why: The proposal is structurally coherent, but its universal scope and removal of a review posture are supported by evidence and alternatives analysis that remain incomplete, with limited safeguards for delay and inconsistent implementation.
pass_5_most_important_consequence: A final rule could increase RFEs, processing delays, and uncertainty for employers and workers before USCIS has a demonstrated monitoring and correction framework for the broader Form I-129 population.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The proposal removes the existing deference requirement but does not add a replacement standard for when prior approvals should receive weight, how repetitive requests should be limited, or how increased RFE and delay effects will be corrected.

evidence.section: III. Discussion of Proposed Rule / Costs to the Federal Government
evidence.quote_or_absence: The proposal says officers may still consider a prior approval where relevant, but the available record does not specify a governing standard or monitoring and correction framework; it also predicts greater RFE use and backlog pressure.

pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask USCIS to adopt review criteria, documentation requirements, supervisory controls, and public metrics before or alongside implementation.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The notice projects more RFEs and an average 64-day processing difference for petitions with RFEs, creating employment-planning and status uncertainty before final adjudication.

evidence.section: Cost-Benefit Analysis / Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis
evidence.quote_or_absence: Based on the average of the last four fiscal years, the difference in processing time between petitions with and without an RFE is 64 days; petitioners may experience longer adjudication times and increased uncertainty regarding continued employment.

pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask for transition rules, expedited handling criteria, and metrics to prevent avoidable employment disruption while a petition is pending.
